Kidney & Urinary Disorders

Kidney and urinary disorders including renal failure, nephritis, urinary retention, and urinary tract infections.

🎯 After this chapter you can

  • Describe common renal and urinary disorders
  • Describe nursing care for patients with renal failure
  • Explain dialysis and pre/post-operative care for renal patients

In simple terms

Renal and urinary disorders affect the kidneys, ureters, bladder and urethra. They can cause pain, difficulty urinating, fluid retention, and life-threatening complications if not treated promptly.

Nurses play a key role in monitoring fluid balance, monitoring urine output, and supporting patients undergoing dialysis.

Common renal & urinary disorders

Disorder Cause/Features Key signs
Acute kidney injury Sudden loss of kidney function Decreased urine output, fluid overload, electrolyte imbalance
Chronic kidney disease Progressive loss of kidney function Fatigue, swelling, nausea, itching
Glomerulonephritis Inflammation of glomeruli Hematuria, proteinuria, edema, hypertension
Urinary tract infection Bacterial infection of urinary tract Dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain
Urinary retention Inability to empty bladder Lower abdominal pain, distended bladder
Benign prostatic hyperplasia Enlarged prostate in men Difficulty urinating, weak stream, nocturia

Nursing care

  • Fluid balance — monitor intake and output strictly; record all fluids in and out
  • Daily weight — sudden weight gain indicates fluid retention
  • Urinary catheter care — maintain sterile technique, keep drainage bag below bladder level, measure output hourly
  • Dialysis care — monitor access site, check blood pressure before/during/after dialysis, assess for disequilibrium syndrome
  • Patient education — fluid restriction, sodium restriction, medication adherence, signs of infection

🔴 Fluid balance is critical

Strict intake and output monitoring is essential for patients with renal disorders. Report oliguria (urine output <0.5 mL/kg/hour) immediately.

Where the nurse uses this

  • Fluid management — record all intake and output; weigh patient daily at same time
  • Catheter care — maintain closed drainage system; empty bag regularly; measure output
  • Dialysis care — monitor access site for infection; assess for disequilibrium syndrome
  • Dietary restrictions — support patient with fluid, sodium, potassium and protein restrictions
  • Patient education — teach signs of infection, medication adherence, fluid restrictions

🔴 Most important for exams

  1. Renal disorders include AKI, CKD, glomerulonephritis, UTI, urinary retention and BPH.
  2. Strict intake and output monitoring is essential for patients with renal disorders.
  3. Urinary catheter care requires aseptic technique and drainage bag below bladder level.
  4. Daily weight monitoring detects fluid retention early.
  5. Dialysis access site must be assessed for infection and patency.
  6. Fluid, sodium, potassium and protein restrictions are common for renal patients.

⭐ Important for exams

  1. Oliguria (urine output <0.5 mL/kg/hour) must be reported immediately.
  2. Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome symptoms: headache, nausea, confusion, seizures.
  3. AV fistula must not be used for blood pressure measurement or blood draws.
  4. UTI prevention: encourage fluids, perineal hygiene, timely voiding.
  5. BPH management: avoid decongestants, encourage regular voiding.

📌 Memory trick

Renal nursing: FIDO — Fluid balance, Infection control, Dialysis access, Output monitoring.

60-second revision

  • Renal disorders: AKI, CKD, glomerulonephritis, UTI, urinary retention, BPH.
  • Strict intake and output monitoring.
  • Urinary catheter: aseptic technique, bag below bladder level.
  • Dialysis: monitor access site, check for disequilibrium syndrome.
  • Fluid, sodium, potassium and protein restrictions common.
  • Oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/hour) must be reported immediately.

Test yourself

Oliguria is defined as urine output:

Answer: B. Oliguria is urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/hour and must be reported immediately.

Urinary catheter drainage bag should be:

Answer: B. The drainage bag must be kept below the bladder level to prevent backflow and infection.

AV fistula should NOT be used for:

Answer: D. AV fistula should not be used for BP measurement, blood draws or infusions to protect the access site.

Glomerulonephritis signs include:

Answer: B. Glomerulonephritis presents with hematuria (blood in urine) and proteinuria (protein in urine).

BPH (benign prostatic hyperplasia) causes:

Answer: A. BPH causes urinary retention due to enlarged prostate compressing the urethra.
